analysis.one_liner: Closes the fracking loophole in the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires companies to disclose the chemicals they inject underground.
analysis.headline: The fracking regulation bill never got a hearing or a vote, sitting in committee until the two-year Congress ended despite 63 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Hydraulic fracturing — fracking — was largely exempt from the Safe Drinking Water Act's rules on what gets pumped underground. This bill would repeal that exemption, require companies to disclose, before and after each fracking operation, the chemicals they inject and in what volumes, post those lists publicly, and hand the chemical formula to doctors during a medical emergency, even when it is a trade secret. It never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink water from the aquifers beneath them. They would gain the right to know which chemicals are being injected underground in their area, and doctors treating a sick or injured worker or resident could get the chemical identity needed for treatment without first satisfying a confidentiality agreement.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption that lets fracking injections escape the underground-injection rules that apply to other activities, bringing fracking under EPA or state program oversight [S2][S3].

Requires operators to disclose the chemicals intended for each operation — including chemical constituents, CAS numbers, safety data sheets, and volumes — before drilling begins, and the chemicals actually used within 30 days after it ends, with the state or EPA posting the lists on a public website [S2][S3].

Requires disclosure of a proprietary or trade-secret chemical formula to the state, EPA, or a treating physician or nurse during a medical emergency, without a prior written statement of need or confidentiality agreement, so treatment is not delayed by paperwork [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies that frack. They would bear the cost of tracking and reporting every chemical used in each operation, of meeting underground-injection permitting requirements where they had previously been exempt, and of losing some ability to shield trade-secret formulas during emergencies.

drawbacks.text: Bringing fracking under the Safe Drinking Water Act would add permitting, reporting, and compliance costs for drillers, and opponents argued this slows domestic oil and gas production and raises energy costs (the same exemption Congress granted in 2005 to keep fracking governed by states rather than federal water-injection rules).

The bill does not go as far as its title suggests on secrecy: it explicitly does not authorize public disclosure of proprietary chemical formulas, so companies could keep the exact formulas confidential from the public in all but medical emergencies [S3].
Chemical disclosure lists what went into the well but does not by itself clean up contamination or compensate anyone harmed; it is a transparency measure layered on top of existing enforcement tools.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is mostly informational: residents near fracking sites would learn what chemicals are injected underground, and doctors could get the identity of a trade-secret chemical in an emergency without delay. The cost falls on drilling companies in the form of reporting and permitting obligations, which supporters saw as modest and opponents as a drag on production. The bill also protects trade secrets outside emergencies, which blunts but does not erase its transparency value. The main reason the bill failed was not its design but that it never received any committee action.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which sent it to its environment subcommittee, and then no hearing, markup, or vote ever happened before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Representative Diana DeGette of Colorado introduced the bill on March 19, 2015, joined by one Republican cosponsor, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Environment and the Economy, and that is the last action recorded in the entire Congress [S5].
The bill drew 63 cosponsors — 62 Democrats and 1 Republican — but never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies kept the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption that shields fracking from underground-injection rules, and faced no federal chemical-disclosure mandate from this bill.

sides.party_line_note: All 62 identifiable partisan cosponsors were Democrats; the single Republican cosponsor, Rep. Chris Gibson of New York, was the only cross-party supporter [S4][S1].

industries.industry: Oil and gas drillers using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: The bill strips the industry's exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act underground-injection rules and requires it to disclose, pre- and post-operation, every chemical it injects and in what volume, including during medical emergencies. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption and its chemical inputs confidential runs against residents who want to know what is being pumped under their land. Trade-secret protection remains intact outside emergencies, which is why the effect is 'loses' rather than an end to the industry's information advantage.

industries.industry: Oil and gas service companies supplying fracking chemicals
industries.note: Suppliers of chemical additives would face reporting requirements for their products' constituents and could lose some trade-secret shield in emergencies, but the bill expressly does not require public disclosure of proprietary formulas, limiting the exposure. Their interest in confidentiality runs against communities and doctors seeking chemical information.
